findings.paper_title: Revenue Outturn Report 2025-26 EIA CABINET REPORT
findings.headline: Interest costs £956k over budget due to delayed capital receipts forcing short-term borrowing
findings.detail: Interest payable on borrowing overran budget by £956k due to additional costs of servicing short-term debt. The council had to resort to short-term borrowing because capital receipt income (from asset sales) was slower than anticipated, creating a cashflow gap that had to be financed at higher cost.
findings.matters: Slower than expected capital receipts forced unplanned short-term borrowing at premium cost. This indicates either optimistic receipt forecasting or exposure to property market volatility. For a lender, it signals the council's sensitivity to capital receipt timing and the cost of being wrong.
findings.figures: £956k additional interest payable variance
findings.quote: Additional cost of servicing short term borrowing, following slower than anticipated house sales.

findings.paper_title: Revenue Outturn Report 2025-26 EIA CABINET REPORT
findings.headline: Housing benefit demand: £405k unfunded cost for temporary and supported accommodation
findings.detail: The council incurred £405k additional costs for housing benefits on temporary and supported accommodation that does not qualify for Department for Work and Pensions subsidy. This is an external demand pressure driven by increased homelessness and housing need beyond budget assumptions, without corresponding central government funding.
findings.matters: This uncontrollable external cost pressure reflects the council's exposure to unfunded homelessness costs. Growing demand for temporary housing without matching subsidy creates a structural local financial pressure that will recur and is difficult to manage down.
findings.figures: £405k additional housing benefit cost for temporary and supported accommodation
findings.quote: The level of Housing Benefits paid out in respect of Temporary and Supported Accommodation that is not eligible for subsidy from the DWP is higher than planned.

findings.paper_title: Revenue Outturn Report 2025-26 EIA CABINET REPORT
findings.headline: Crematorium income £486k below budget, including £200k VAT rate budgeting error
findings.detail: Cremation fee income fell £486k short of plan. The shortfall breaks down as: £200k attributable to fees budgeted at standard VAT rate when incorrect, and £286k additional demand shortfall in-year. The VAT rate error indicates a quality issue in budget preparation; the demand shortfall suggests declining service usage.
findings.matters: The £200k VAT rate error represents a governance weakness in budget review processes. Combined with £286k actual demand shortfall, this is a material risk on a previously reliable revenue line, and it came to light only in outturn.
findings.figures: Cremation fees £486k below plan (£200k VAT rate error, £286k demand shortfall)
findings.quote: This is due to fees budgeted incorrectly at the standard rate of VAT, which equates to £200k and an additional shortfall in year of £286k.

findings.paper_title: Revenue Outturn Report 2025-26 EIA CABINET REPORT
findings.headline: Leisure facilities overspend of £822k following in-house takeover of ALIVE centres
findings.detail: Multiple leisure venues significantly exceeded budget following the return of ALIVE leisure services to borough council management during the year. Alive Lynnsport overspent by £376k (driven by £242k business rates increase, plus £90k maintenance and £28k utilities). Alive Oasis overspent £133k. The pattern across multiple venues suggests the outsourced model was substantially cheaper to operate than council in-house running.
findings.matters: A £822k leisure overspend (3% of total service spend) indicates material budget management risk. The jump in property costs following in-house takeover raises questions about the council's forward cost forecasting and the long-term viability of operating these facilities directly.
findings.figures: Alive Lynnsport £376k overspend (business rates £242k, maintenance £90k), Alive Oasis £133k, total Leisure and Community Facilities £822k
findings.quote: Business rates increase by £242k following return of service to Borough Council management.

findings.paper_title: capital outturn report 25-26
findings.headline: Levelling Up Fund withdrawn from Southgate Regeneration scheme, causing planning delays
findings.detail: The Southgate Regeneration Area experienced delays in 2025/26 following removal of Levelling Up Fund scheme funding. This loss of external grant funding reduced the council's ability to progress the scheme as originally budgeted.
findings.matters: Loss of government grant funding reduces the council's financial capacity and extends the delivery timeline for regeneration, with implications for local economic impact and debt servicing duration.
findings.figures: Delay to Southgate Regeneration Area scheme
findings.quote: Costs were less than budgeted due delay in progressing planning for the scheme following removal of the Levelling Up Fund scheme funding.

findings.paper_title: capital outturn report 25-26
findings.headline: Temporary borrowing of £17.3m in 2025/26 with £20.3m required in 2026/27; interest rates rising
findings.detail: The council is using temporary borrowing for cash flow management: £17.3m in 2025/26 and projected £20.3m in 2026/27. The report notes that PWLB and external loan rates are 'at a higher rate due to the current Bank of England base rate and increasing demand for public sector borrowing combined with worldwide issues such as war which has an impact on bank rates.' This temporary borrowing rolls over annually and creates refinancing risk.
findings.matters: For debt sustainability, a lender needs to understand both the stock of debt and the cost trajectory. High temporary borrowing creates annual refinancing risk, and rising rates mean debt servicing costs will increase materially.
findings.figures: £17.3m temporary borrowing 2025/26; £20.3m projected 2026/27; £3.5m unsupported borrowing 2026/27
findings.quote: The interest rates of external loans and PWLB loans are at a higher rate due to the current Bank of England base rate and increasing demand for public sector borrowing combined with worldwide issues such as war which has an impact on bank rates.

findings.paper_title: capital outturn report 25-26
findings.headline: Capital receipts of £50m from major housing projects represent 100% of general fund reserve balance across 5-year period, rated high risk
findings.detail: The council's entire 2025-2030 capital programme financing strategy depends on achieving £50m in capital receipts from major housing projects. The report explicitly states this sum represents 100% of the current general fund reserve balance and assigns it a 'High' risk rating. The council notes this is 'a challenging target in the current economic climate' given that the housing market may slow and sales may not be achieved as planned.
findings.matters: For a lender assessing creditworthiness, this concentration of dependency is material: if housing sales fall short or the market deteriorates, the council has zero financial buffer and must take on additional unplanned borrowing to deliver its capital plan.
findings.figures: £50m expected total; £6.7m achieved in 2025/26 (mostly £5.9m from housing sales); 100% of current general fund reserve balance
findings.quote: Capital receipts over the 5-year capital programme 2025-2030 represent 100% of the current general fund reserve balance... The sum total of capital receipts included in the funding table of circ. £50m is from the Major Housing Project, it's a challenging target in the current economic climate.

findings.paper_title: capital outturn report 25-26
findings.headline: Florence Fields major housing project £0.71m behind schedule due to ground investigations requiring additional piling
findings.detail: Phase 6 of Florence Fields, the council's largest housing development project, has been significantly delayed by ground investigations necessitating additional piling works. The project end date may need to be extended and wet weather also caused lost days. This is one of the core schemes generating the capital receipts the council depends on to fund its entire capital programme.
findings.matters: A lender needs to understand delays and cost pressures in the schemes that generate the £50m in capital receipts underpinning the entire 2025-2030 capital plan—if these projects slip or fail to generate expected sales, the council has no reserves to bridge the gap.
findings.figures: £0.71m behind profile in 2025/26; Florence Fields is 226 total homes across multiple phases
findings.quote: Phase 6 progress has been impacted by ground investigations with a requirement for additional piling, this delayed progress on site and final end date may need to be extended, in addition days were lost due to wet weather.

findings.paper_title: 20260615 Audit Committee Draft 2026 Annual Governance Statement
findings.headline: Some services experiencing challenges in recruitment, retention and capacity, with incomplete statutory training compliance.
findings.detail: The council identifies that some services continue to experience challenges in recruitment, retention and capacity which affects resilience and service delivery. Statutory training compliance is not consistent across all areas, with partial completion or unclear interpretation in some teams, suggesting staff may not be aware of required training.
findings.matters: Workforce capacity challenges and training gaps reduce service resilience and increase operational and compliance risk; capacity constraints may impair financial management and audit readiness.
findings.figures: Partial completion of statutory training in some services; challenges in recruitment and retention affect resilience
findings.quote: Some services continue to experience challenges in recruitment, retention, and capacity, which affects resilience and service delivery. In addition, statutory training compliance is not yet consistent across all areas, with partial completion or unclear interpretation in some teams.

findings.paper_title: 20260615 Audit Committee Draft 2026 Annual Governance Statement
findings.headline: Local Government Reorganisation presents major transition risks requiring maintenance of business-as-usual performance whilst delivering structural change.
findings.detail: The forthcoming Local Government Reorganisation (LGR) with shadow unitary authority establishment in May 2027 and vesting day 1 April 2028 represents a major transition. The council recognises that delivering major structural change whilst maintaining reliable day-to-day services creates unavoidable risks; the scale of transformation may place pressure on capacity and established processes.
findings.matters: Major organisational restructuring creates execution risk to service delivery and financial management; capacity constraints during LGR could impair the council's ability to manage finances and respond to challenges.
findings.figures: Shadow unitary authority May 2027; Vesting Day 1 April 2028
findings.quote: LGR brings unavoidable risks as the Council must deliver major structural change while continuing to provide reliable day-to-day services. The scale of transformation may place pressure on capacity and established processes, so maintaining strong oversight and protecting business‑as‑usual performance will remain essential throughout 2026/27.

findings.paper_title: 20260615 Audit Committee Draft 2026 Annual Governance Statement
findings.headline: Significant risks identified in information governance, data protection and data management with lack of ownership across digital systems.
findings.detail: An application review in January-March 2026 identified that the organisation was carrying significant risks related to Information Governance, Data Protection and data management practices. A lack of ownership and accountability was found for a number of digital systems, with compliance issues around retention schedules, statutory response timeframes, and maintenance of Records of Processing Activity.
findings.matters: Data governance weaknesses create cyber and data protection compliance risk; lack of system ownership suggests control environment gaps that could affect service continuity and regulatory compliance.
findings.figures: Application review January-March 2026; revised Data Protection Policy to be presented to Cabinet June 2026
findings.quote: An application review was conducted during January, February and March 2026, which highlighted a lack of ownership and accountability for a number of digital systems being used across the authority, with no one seemingly being responsible for the data held in those systems.

findings.paper_title: 20260615 Audit Committee Draft 2026 Annual Governance Statement
findings.headline: Health and safety system assessed as under strain with inconsistent processes, identified as a significant governance issue.
findings.detail: An external review by Bureau Veritas found the current health and safety system is under strain due to inconsistent processes and historic working practices that have created gaps requiring organisation-wide attention. The report notes the issue is not lack of willingness but lack of consistent structure, capacity and communication. An 18-month action plan has been put in place and is monitored monthly.
findings.matters: Health and safety control weaknesses create operational and reputational risk; strain on systems due to capacity issues may indicate broader organisational resilience concerns.
findings.figures: 18-month action plan; Health and Safety Board meets monthly
findings.quote: the current health & safety system is under strain due to inconsistent processes and historic ways of working that has created gaps that need to be coordinated and given organisation wide attention

findings.paper_title: 20260615 Audit Committee Draft 2026 Annual Governance Statement
findings.headline: Areas of non-compliant procurement spend identified as a significant governance issue.
findings.detail: The council has identified areas where procurement activity did not fully comply with Contract Standing Orders or national procurement regulations. A deep dive review was commenced at the end of quarter four to understand root causes and drive improvements. Non-compliant spend is assessed as a significant governance issue because Contract Standing Orders are essential protection against fraud, corruption, and ensuring value for money.
findings.matters: Non-compliance with procurement controls indicates breakdown in internal governance framework, creating fraud risk and suggesting some spend may not represent best value.
findings.figures: Non-compliant spend identified through quarterly P&CTM meetings; deep dive review commenced end of Q4
findings.quote: There are areas of non-compliant spend, Contract Standing Orders are an internal control designed to support best value being achieved and as a protection against fraud & corruption. They are an essential part of the Governance Framework.

findings.paper_title: 20260615 Audit Committee Draft 2026 Annual Governance Statement
findings.headline: Budget gaps confirmed from 2026/27 onwards with reliance on reserve drawdown and savings delivery.
findings.detail: The Medium-Term Financial Strategy presented in February 2026 confirms that budget gaps persist from 2026/27 onwards due to continued uncertainty in national local government finance and cost/demand pressures. The council plans to address gaps through a phased use of reserves, income generation, service redesign, transformation, and savings delivery.
findings.matters: Persistent budget gaps requiring reserve drawdown signal underlying financial sustainability challenges; successful delivery of savings programmes is critical to maintain financial resilience.
findings.figures: Budget gaps persist from 2026/27 onwards
findings.quote: The MTFS presented to Cabinet and Full Council in February 2026 confirms that budget gaps persist from 2026/27 onwards, reflecting continued uncertainty in the national local government finance system and the scale of cost and demand pressures. To achieve longer term financial sustainability, a combination of measures will be required during the next budget cycle, including a phased but time limited use of reserves, income generation, service redesign and transformation, and the delivery of savings.

findings.paper_title: 20260615 Audit Committee Draft 2026 Annual Governance Statement
findings.headline: External auditors issued a disclaimer of opinion on the 2024/25 accounts and identified a significant governance weakness in financial reporting.
findings.detail: Ernst & Young issued a disclaimer of opinion on the financial statements for the year ended 31 March 2025, unable to obtain sufficient audit evidence due to backlog and delays. The auditors identified a significant weakness in governance relating to preparation of the Statement of Accounts and provision of high-quality supporting working papers. Disclaimer opinions have also been issued for 2021 through 2024.
findings.matters: A disclaimer opinion means the council's financial position cannot be independently verified; lenders cannot rely on audited accounts, and this reflects systemic capacity or control failures in finance function.
findings.figures: Disclaimer issued for years ended 31 March 2021, 2022, 2023, 2024, and 2025
findings.quote: The auditors issued a disclaimer of opinion on the financial statements, reflecting that they were unable to obtain sufficient appropriate audit evidence due to ongoing audit backlog issues, delays in the provision of supporting information and the impact of prior year disclaimers.

findings.paper_title: Treasury Strategy 2026-27 Council
findings.headline: IFRS 16 lease accounting adoption will further increase CFR and long-term liabilities
findings.detail: The council has adopted IFRS 16, which requires recognition of lease assets and liabilities on the balance sheet. This creates a one-off increase to the CFR and an increase to the council's recorded debt liability, with an equivalent MRP charge to reduce the liability.
findings.matters: While the accounting treatment is neutral to cash flow, it increases the recorded indebtedness and CFR figures. The exact quantum is not disclosed in this document, but it will add to the debt burden already growing 37% over the forecast period.
findings.figures: No specific quantum disclosed; described as retrospective accounting requiring MRP charge.
findings.quote: Generally accepted accounting practice requires changes introduced by IFRS 16 to be accounted for retrospectively. Consequently, an element of the rental or service charge payable in previous years (and previously charged to revenue accounts) will be taken to the balance sheet to reduce the liability.

findings.paper_title: Treasury Strategy 2026-27 Council
findings.headline: Council strategy depends on interest rate falls that may not materialise
findings.detail: The council is maintaining an under-borrowed position, using cash reserves instead of borrowing, betting that longer-dated rates will fall from current levels (PWLB 5yr at 4.81%, 25yr at 6.01%). If rates rise or fall more slowly than forecast, borrowing costs will be higher than anticipated.
findings.matters: This is an interest rate directional bet. A prolonged high-rate environment would force the council to borrow at elevated costs or deplete reserves faster. The forecast assumes rates fall 25-70 bps over 2-4 years, which is not guaranteed.
findings.figures: Current PWLB rates: 5-year 4.81%, 10-year 5.39%, 25-year 6.01%. Target rate 5-year (end Q4 2027): 4.10%.
findings.quote: This strategy is prudent as medium and longer dated borrowing rates are expected to fall from their current levels, albeit only once prevailing inflation concerns are addressed by restrictive near-term monetary policy.

findings.paper_title: Treasury Strategy 2026-27 Council
findings.headline: Aggressive capital expenditure programme with large tier 1 commitments but insufficient capital resources
findings.detail: Total capital expenditure for 2026/27 reaches £70.4m (including pipeline schemes exempt from normal approval), with £45.4m in major tier 1 projects alone. Capital receipts, grants, and reserves can only fund £49.7m of this, leaving £3.3m in unsupported borrowing required.
findings.matters: The scale of unsupported borrowing needed (growing from £1.9m to £3.3m) indicates capital expenditure is outpacing the council's own resource generation. This depends on external borrowing to complete the programme.
findings.figures: Total capital 2026/27: £70,367,960; Tier 1 Major Projects: £45,435,420; Unsupported Borrowing: £3,312,730.
findings.quote: Tier 1: Major Projects 45,435,420 [...] Unsupported Borrowing 3,312,730

findings.paper_title: Treasury Strategy 2026-27 Council
findings.headline: Capital financing costs jump 25% as proportion of revenue in 2026/27
findings.detail: The Ratio of Financing Costs to Net Revenue Stream rises from 5.81% in 2025/26 to 7.30% in 2026/27, then moderates to around 5.6-6.3% for later years. This reflects the impact of the capital programme beginning to be financed through new borrowing.
findings.matters: A large increase in debt service costs relative to revenue reduces financial flexibility and indicates the capital programme is demanding a higher proportion of available resources. If revenues fall or costs rise, serviceability could tighten quickly.
findings.figures: Financing costs 2025/26: 5.81% of net revenue; 2026/27: 7.30% of net revenue.
findings.quote: Ratio of Financing Costs to Net Revenue Stream 5.81% 7.30%

findings.paper_title: Treasury Strategy 2026-27 Council
findings.headline: Debt burden more than triples over five years
findings.detail: External borrowings are projected to grow from £19.6m in 2025/26 to £63.8m in 2029/30. The Capital Financing Requirement rises from £77.8m to £106.6m over the same period, increasing the council's total indebtedness by 37%.
findings.matters: This material increase in leverage materially changes the council's debt profile and financial risk. Lenders need to understand whether this is sustainable relative to revenue growth and whether these capital assets will generate sufficient returns.
findings.figures: External borrowings: £19.625m to £63.767m. CFR: £77,772k to £106,591k. Net financing need 2026/27: £19,067,530.
findings.quote: Expected external borrowings 19,625 27,174 47,603 61,150 63,767

findings.paper_title: Treasury Strategy 2026-27 Council
findings.headline: Rapid reserve depletion alongside aggressive capital spending
findings.detail: General fund balances and earmarked reserves are forecast to decline from £42.7m in 2026/27 to £29.4m in 2029/30—a 31% reduction over four years. This occurs while capital expenditure jumps from £40.3m to £70.4m in 2026/27 and the council commits £3.3m in unsupported borrowing for that year.
findings.matters: Declining liquidity while debt grows significantly raises questions about financial sustainability and the council's ability to absorb shocks or fund unforeseen capital needs.
findings.figures: Reserves fall from £42,739k to £29,407k (2026/27 to 2029/30); unsupported borrowing rises to £3,312,730 in 2026/27.
findings.quote: General fund balances / ear marked reserves (38,546) (42,739) (39,254) (34,170) (29,407)

findings.paper_title: 202425 Borough Council of Kings Lynn & West Norfolk - EY Audit Results Report
findings.headline: Finance team capacity insufficient to support audit timetable; delays in accessing finance officers and responses from non-finance staff
findings.detail: While not encountering major access issues with the finance team itself, the auditors noted the overall capacity of the finance team to support the audit resulted in delays. Additionally, there were issues accessing and receiving responses from officers outside the finance team.
findings.matters: Insufficient finance team capacity constrains the council's ability to manage its financial affairs, complete timely close procedures, and respond to audit or lender information requests.
findings.figures: Not specified
findings.quote: Overall, we did not encounter significant issues with access to the finance team, but the overall capacity of the finance team to support the audit has resulted in delays to the audit process.

findings.paper_title: 202425 Borough Council of Kings Lynn & West Norfolk - EY Audit Results Report
findings.headline: Identified significant weakness in Value for Money arrangements: Council's ability to produce reliable and timely financial reporting
findings.detail: Auditors identified a significant weakness in the council's VFM arrangements, specifically its ability to produce reliable and timely financial reporting that supports strategic priorities and enables financial statement audit. The weakness stems from ongoing operational and resourcing difficulties over several years impacting accounts preparation timeliness and audit of historic financial statements.
findings.matters: A VFM audit finding on financial reporting capability signals systemic weaknesses in the council's management and governance that affect all stakeholders including lenders.
findings.figures: Affects financial reporting dating back to 2019/20 accounts
findings.quote: The Council has faced ongoing operational and resourcing difficulties over several years impacting the timeliness of accounts preparation and the audit of historic financial statements

findings.paper_title: 202425 Borough Council of Kings Lynn & West Norfolk - EY Audit Results Report
findings.headline: Draft financial statements published 14 days late (14 July vs 30 June deadline) due to incomplete accounting entries for PPE and pensions
findings.detail: The council failed to meet the 30 June 2025 statutory publication deadline, publishing accounts on 14 July 2025 instead. The delay was caused by incomplete accounting entries relating to valuation of Property, Plant & Equipment and Pensions. A formal Notice of Delay was issued.
findings.matters: Late publication signals control weaknesses in financial close procedures and hinders timely decision-making by lenders and regulators.
findings.figures: Deadline 30 June 2025; actual publication 14 July 2025; 14-day delay
findings.quote: The financial statements were not published by the 30 June 2025 deadline set out in the Accounts and Audit Regulations. This was due to incomplete accounting entries relating to the valuation of Property, Plant & Equipment and Pensions. The required Notice of Delay was issued and the Statement of Accounts were subsequently published on 14 July 2025.

findings.paper_title: 202425 Borough Council of Kings Lynn & West Norfolk - EY Audit Results Report
findings.headline: Church Street car park investment property overvalued by minimum £0.4 million; Council's valuers use non-standard yield methodology
findings.detail: Auditor's internal valuers determined that Church Street car park, valued at £3.2 million, has been valued using yields that are too optimistic compared to comparable investment transactions. The overstatement is at least £0.4 million. Additionally, the council's external valuers use a non-standard gross yield approach while the UK market standard is net yields including purchaser costs, making comparisons to market data difficult and requiring additional audit procedures.
findings.matters: Material overvaluation of income-producing assets directly affects the apparent financial position and loan repayment capacity.
findings.figures: Church Street car park recorded at £3.2m, minimum overstatement £0.4m
findings.quote: Church Street car park is recorded in the financial statements at £3.2 million. Our internal valuers have determined that the yield applied to this asset's valuation is too optimistic when compared to comparable investment transactions. This results in an overstatement in the valuation of the asset by a minimum of £0.4 million as at 31 March 2025.

findings.paper_title: 202425 Borough Council of Kings Lynn & West Norfolk - EY Audit Results Report
findings.headline: Investment property portfolio of £68.4 million includes £29.4 million of potentially duplicated industrial assets that auditor could not verify
findings.detail: The council holds £68.4 million in investment properties, including £29.4 million of industrial properties grouped in the asset register. Auditors noted potential duplication and requested a breakdown of individual industrial assets but the council could not provide it, preventing audit procedures from being completed. For retail assets tested, the council could not provide lease documentation to support valuations.
findings.matters: A material income-generating asset base that cannot be verified or even individually identified raises questions about asset management and income reliability.
findings.figures: Total investment properties £68.4m; industrial properties £29.4m; non-industrial assets £39.0m
findings.quote: The 2024/25 financial statements discloses £68.4 million of Investment Property assets on the Balance Sheet. We identified that £29.4 million of the Investment Property balance relates to industrial properties which are grouped together in the Council's fixed asset register. Upon review of these industrial assets we noted some potential duplication of the assets being valued and we requested a breakdown of the industrial assets to enable us to select and test individual assets, but officers have been unable to provide this breakdown.

findings.paper_title: 202425 Borough Council of Kings Lynn & West Norfolk - EY Audit Results Report
findings.headline: Capital assets register and general ledger contain unreconciled differences of £0.8 million and £11.0 million classification error
findings.detail: During testing of capital accounting entries, auditors identified a £0.8 million unreconciled difference between the fixed asset register and the council's general ledger, and an £11.0 million difference in how assets are classified between the financial statements and the fixed asset register. The council was unable to adequately respond to audit queries or support these differences, leaving the audit procedures incomplete.
findings.matters: Unreconciled capital balances of this magnitude suggest control failures over asset recording and raise questions about which figures are accurate.
findings.figures: £0.8m unreconciled difference; £11.0m classification difference; £3.6m impairment in Assets Under Construction
findings.quote: A £0.8 million unreconciled difference between the total in the fixed asset register and the Council's general ledger. An £11.0 million classification difference between the categories of assets in the financial statements and the Council's fixed asset register.

findings.paper_title: 202425 Borough Council of Kings Lynn & West Norfolk - EY Audit Results Report
findings.headline: Pension asset overstated by £31.6 million due to failure to apply asset ceiling requirement; prior years also misstated
findings.detail: The council recorded a pension asset of £28.2 million in 2023/24 when it should have been a liability of £1.9 million. In 2024/25, similar errors totalling £31.6 million were identified. Management has not corrected the 2023/24 prior-year error in the 2024/25 accounts. The error arose because management failed to apply IFRIC 14 asset ceiling rules to pension positions in prior years and only obtained the combined IAS19/IFRIC 14 report for 2024/25.
findings.matters: A £30+ million error in how the council values its pension liability calls into question management's financial accounting capability and the reliability of multi-year positions.
findings.figures: 2023/24 pension asset £28.2m should have been £1.9m liability; 2024/25 misstatement £31.6m; 2022/23 pension asset £8.3m
findings.quote: The Council obtained the required combined report for 2024/25 which shows that the pension asset in 2024/25 required adjustment for the asset ceiling by £23.1 million bringing the balance into a liability position of £1.6 million. This combined report also includes the balances for 2023/24 which shows that the pension asset should be reduced to a liability of £1.9 million, therefore indicating a material misstatement in 2023/24 and 2022/23 which would require a prior period adjustment in 2024/25 to correct for. Management have not put through a prior period adjustment in the 2024/25 financial statements and therefore this misstatement remains uncorrected.

findings.paper_title: 202425 Borough Council of Kings Lynn & West Norfolk - EY Audit Results Report
findings.headline: Auditor will disclaim opinion on 2024/25 accounts due to insufficient evidence over material balances and lack of prior-year assurance
findings.detail: The auditor issued disclaimers on 2020/21, 2021/22, 2023/24 financial statements and will disclaim 2024/25 as well. The council has not obtained sufficient evidence to have reasonable assurance over all in-year movements and closing balances. The lack of evidence over prior-year balances and current-year movements, combined with the backdated audit deadline, means the auditor cannot conclude the 2024/25 statements are free from material misstatement.
findings.matters: A disclaimer of opinion means the council's financial position cannot be independently verified, which is a critical prerequisite for any lending decision.
findings.figures: 2024/25 backstop date: 27 February 2026; prior disclaimers issued on 2020/21, 2021/22, 2022/23, 2023/24
findings.quote: We therefore anticipate issuing a disclaimed 2024/25 audit opinion.

findings.paper_title: Capital Strategy 2026-27 Council Draft
findings.headline: Asset Management Strategy under development and may 'fundamentally change' capital programme
findings.detail: The council states it has begun developing an Asset Management Strategy but provides no timeline or draft principles. The document notes: 'The Capital programme may fundamentally change as a result of this document, as it determines the best approach to managing, maintaining and using its assets.'
findings.matters: This signals uncertainty about the council's future capital priorities and spending. A significant asset review could redirect borrowing away from regeneration schemes or toward maintenance, altering debt serviceability projections.
findings.figures: None provided
findings.quote: The Council has begun the process of developing an Asset Management Strategy. The Capital programme may fundamentally change as a result of this document, as it determines the best approach to managing, maintaining and using its assets.

findings.paper_title: Capital Strategy 2026-27 Council Draft
findings.headline: Leisure facilities now council-managed: new financial burden as of April 2025
findings.detail: Four leisure facilities (Lynnsport, St James Swimming Pool, Downham Market Leisure Centre, Oasis Leisure Centre Hunstanton) returned to full council management on 1 April 2025. The council is undertaking a review of upgrading or replacing some facilities, but no budget estimates or timeline are provided.
findings.matters: Leisure operations are typically loss-making and capital-intensive. Taking these in-house removes a contracted management risk but adds direct operational and capital expenditure. Deferred maintenance on leisure facilities is often substantial.
findings.figures: Four facilities affected; no budget stated for upgrade/replacement plans
findings.quote: Leisure facilities and activities at Lynnsport, St James Swimming Pool, Downham Market Leisure Centre and at Oasis Leisure Centre in Hunstanton came back to be fully managed within the Council on 1 April 2025. The council is currently undertaking a review of options for upgrading/replacing of some of the facilities.

findings.paper_title: Capital Strategy 2026-27 Council Draft
findings.headline: Council borrowing to lend to its own housing and property companies
findings.detail: The council has established West Norfolk Housing Ltd and West Norfolk Property Limited, and has been granted delegated authority to borrow and lend to these companies via a drawdown facility. As of 31 December 2025, the council has made £3.1m in capital loans to West Norfolk Housing Company at 4.5% plus base rate. The Treasury Management Strategy sets an investment limit of £50m for wholly owned local authority companies.
findings.matters: This creates exposure to company performance and housing market risk. If these companies underperform or property values fall, the council loses rental income and faces loan impairment risk. The authority is also exposing itself to refinancing risk if it borrows short-term to lend long-term.
findings.figures: Capital loans outstanding: £3.1m at 31 Dec 2025; Interest receivable YTD: £132k; Treasury limit for company investments: £50m
findings.quote: The Council has made loans for capital purposes to West Norfolk Housing Company... The Treasury Management Strategy has an investment treasury indicator and limit for total principal funds invested for greater than 365 days for Wholly Owned Local Authority Companies of £50 million.

findings.paper_title: Capital Strategy 2026-27 Council Draft
findings.headline: Significant unsupported borrowing programme of £48.8m over five years
findings.detail: The council is funding its capital programme substantially through prudential borrowing. Unsupported borrowing (funded from service budgets) accounts for £48.8m of the £148.7m capital programme, with additional temporary borrowing of £6.7m. This represents the largest single financing source after grants.
findings.matters: Revenue costs of servicing this debt will extend 'potentially up to 50 years into the future' and will compound the revenue funding pressures already acknowledged. The S151 Officer must demonstrate affordability.
findings.figures: Unsupported borrowing: £48.8m; Temporary borrowing: £6.7m; Total capital programme: £148.7m
findings.quote: Under the current Prudential Borrowing Code arrangements, the Council can determine its own borrowing limits for capital expenditure... The Capital Strategy requires the Section 151 Officer to report, as part of the annual Budget setting for each year, on the level and the affordability of the prudential borrowing.

findings.paper_title: Capital Strategy 2026-27 Council Draft
findings.headline: Cost-reduction measures acknowledged as insufficient to balance future budgets
findings.detail: The council explicitly states that despite undertaking cost-reduction initiatives to support the phasing out of Revenue Support Grant, 'these do not go far enough to balance its budget in the years ahead.' The council is relying on capital projects linked to strategic objectives to help address its revenue requirements going forward.
findings.matters: This signals a structural revenue deficit that the council cannot close through efficiency measures alone, and indicates the council is using capital investment (regeneration, housing, commercial development) as a revenue-generation strategy.
findings.figures: No specific deficit figure stated. Capital programme 2025-2030 totals £148.7m.
findings.quote: Even though the council has undertaken cost-reduction measures, these do not go far enough to balance its budget in the years ahead. To address this the council has identified projects that link to strategic corporate objectives, help to address its revenue requirements going forward and take advantage of capital funding opportunities being promoted by Central Government.

findings.paper_title: Annual Assurance Report for Audit Committee from the Shareholder 2025
findings.headline: Both the housing and property companies' boards have identified the need for additional dedicated officer resource, particularly a company secretary function
findings.detail: Both WNHC (section 4.2) and WNPL (section 5.2) boards have 'actively discussed and recognised the need for dedicated officer resource to support the Board with its work, particularly around the Company Secretary function.' Officer support is currently provided via SLAs and recharged. This signals capacity strain in current arrangements.
findings.matters: Governance bottlenecks at officer level could delay board decision-making and capital programme delivery; indicates current shared-resource model is at strain point
findings.figures: No figures on resource costs or gaps
findings.quote: the Board has actively discussed and recognised the need for dedicated officer resource to support the Board with its work, particularly around the Company Secretary function.

findings.paper_title: Annual Assurance Report for Audit Committee from the Shareholder 2025
findings.headline: Key performance indicators to hold the companies accountable to the shareholder have not yet been developed
findings.detail: Section 3.2.12 states explicitly that 'KPIs between the Shareholder and WNHC and WNPL need to be developed for inclusion in the Business Plans.' This is a control gap in an otherwise mature governance framework—the council lacks defined performance measures for delivery of strategic objectives.
findings.matters: Without agreed KPIs, the council's ability to hold companies to account for performance and delivery is weakened; affects accountability over capital expenditure and housing delivery timelines
findings.figures: None
findings.quote: KPIs between the Shareholder and WNHC and WNPL need to be developed for inclusion in the Business Plans.

findings.paper_title: Annual Assurance Report for Audit Committee from the Shareholder 2025
findings.headline: The revised Service Level Agreement for WNHC defining council support and cost recovery remains incomplete after review
findings.detail: Section 3.2.11 explicitly notes that the SLA for WNHC 'is still to be reviewed and completed.' SLAs define how the Council provides corporate services (finance, legal, ICT) to the company and recovery of costs. Until finalized, there is uncertainty over the company's cost base.
findings.matters: An unfinalized SLA creates cost uncertainty for the housing company and undefined support obligations for the council; material for both financial planning and control frameworks
findings.figures: No figures given on SLA costs
findings.quote: The revised and updated SLA for WNHC is still to be reviewed and completed.

findings.paper_title: Annual Assurance Report for Audit Committee from the Shareholder 2025
findings.headline: WNHC is acquiring 58 affordable homes in the next 6 months funded by new Council loan facilities still under negotiation
findings.detail: The housing company currently owns 47 homes valued at £5m, funded by £3.2m in existing Council loans. It is about to acquire approximately 58 more homes using a mixture of new loan facilities from the Council and grant funding. Critically, these loan facility agreements have not yet been finalized, only described as 'in negotiation process.'
findings.matters: The council is expanding contingent exposure through subsidiary borrowing; delays in loan agreements could impede the housing pipeline, and the council needs to ensure loan terms are prudent
findings.figures: 47 homes currently owned, £3.2m outstanding Council loans, £5m current valuation, 58 homes incoming, loan facilities 'once agreements are entered'
findings.quote: WNHC is due to acquire approximately 58 affordable homes in the next 6 months by way of a mixture of drawing down on loan facilities with the Council (once agreements are entered) and grant funding.

findings.paper_title: Treasury Outturn Report 2024 2025
findings.headline: Council is using reserves as working capital to cover the £44.9m gap between Capital Financing Requirement and actual borrowing
findings.detail: The CFR is £83.4m but gross borrowing is only £38.5m. The £44.9m gap is covered by net investments (£17m) and reserves (£30.2m earmarked, £8.6m general balances). The council has deliberately maintained an 'under-borrowed position' pending rate falls. This strategy is intentional but means reserves are not being built up and remain at modest absolute levels.
findings.matters: Reserves deployed as a float to defer borrowing reduce financial flexibility for other shocks or unplanned spend. If rate expectations change or capital spend accelerates, the council may face rapid reserve depletion.
findings.figures: CFR £83,431k; gross borrowing £38,500k; gap £44,931k; investments £17,015k; general balances £8,578k
findings.quote: During 2024/25, the Authority maintained an under-borrowed position. This meant that the capital borrowing need, (the Capital Financing Requirement), was not fully funded with loan debt as cash supporting the Authority's reserves, balances and cash flow was used as an interim measure.

findings.paper_title: Treasury Outturn Report 2024 2025
findings.headline: Borrowing strategy depends entirely on Bank Rate falling to reduce refinancing costs; forecasts have already been wrong once
findings.detail: The council explicitly chose short-term, lower-rate borrowing betting on rate falls. Section 7.4 states the strategy was prudent because long-term borrowing costs 'are expected to fall back through 2025 and 2026'. However, the report admits: 'Forecasts were too optimistic from a rate reduction perspective' in 2024. Bank Rate stands at 4.5% as of March 2025, down from 5.25%, but further cuts are uncertain.
findings.matters: If interest rate expectations reverse again (as they did in 2024), this strategy leaves the council exposed to refinancing at materially higher costs. A lender would want confidence the council has contingency plans.
findings.figures: Bank Rate at 4.5% March 2025 (down from 5.25% peak); short-term borrowing at 5.5-5.8%; PWLB 1-year rate 4.82% at year-end
findings.quote: This strategy was prudent as although near-term investment rates were equal to, and sometimes higher than, long-term borrowing costs, the latter are expected to fall back through 2025 and 2026 in the light of economic growth concerns and the eventual dampening of inflation. The Authority has sought to minimise the taking on of long-term borrowing at elevated levels (>5%).

findings.paper_title: Treasury Outturn Report 2024 2025
findings.headline: £28.5m (74% of debt) matures within 12 months, creating significant refinancing risk in 2025
findings.detail: As at 31 March 2025, three short-term loans totalling £28.5m mature during 2025: £5m in April, £3.5m in May, and £20m PWLB facility in March 2026. These will need to be refinanced or repaid from reserves. Short-term borrowing rates were 5.5-5.8%, and the PWLB at 4.86%, all higher than historical norms.
findings.matters: Heavy refinancing requirements mean the council faces significant exposure to interest rate risk in 2025. If rates do not fall as expected, refinancing costs could be substantially higher, or the council may need to draw reserves to repay rather than refinance.
findings.quote: As at the 31 March 2025 the council had three short-term loans with a collective value of £28,500,000, these mature during 2025.

findings.paper_title: Treasury Outturn Report 2024 2025
findings.headline: Gross borrowing more than doubled from £15m to £38.5m in a single year
findings.detail: The council added £23.5m of new debt in 2024/2025, a 157% increase year-on-year. This comprises a £20m PWLB facility at 4.86%, two short-term loans from Middlesbrough Teeside Pension Fund (£5m at 5.5%, £3.5m at 5.8%), and £8.5m with other Local Authorities at 5.65%. The council states this was for capital purposes only.
findings.matters: A tripling of debt volume in one year is significant. For a lender assessing the council, this represents a material step-change in leverage and requires confidence that capital programmes justify this level of borrowing.
findings.quote: £20,000,000 was drawn from the PWLB to fund unfinanced capital expenditure, this is also classed as short-term as it the maturity is 12 months.

findings.paper_title: Treasury Outturn Report 2024 2025
findings.headline: Capital Financing Requirement jumped by £18m in one year to £83.4m, driven by £20.4m of unfinanced capital expenditure
findings.detail: The council's underlying borrowing need (CFR) rose from £65.4m to £83.4m. Of £39.7m capital spending, only £19.2m was financed in-year; the remaining £20.4m remains unfinanced and is being met through borrowing and reserve drawdown. Even with £2.4m of Minimum Revenue Provision repayment, the CFR grew by 27.6%.
findings.matters: A CFR growing at 27% annually is material. If this rate continues, the council's debt serviceability could become a concern for lenders, particularly if capital programmes do not moderate.
findings.figures: CFR opening balance £65,379k, closing £83,431k; unfinanced capital expenditure £20,431k; capital financing requirement increase of £18,052k
findings.quote: The Council's CFR for the year is shown below and represents a key prudential indicator. It includes leasing schemes that are on the balance sheet, as these increase the Council's borrowing need.
